qs.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a firm mass in the sigmoid colon. Colonoscopy shows an ulcerated lesion with irregular borders. Biopsy demonstrates invasion through the muscularis propria. Which histological feature most strongly distinguishes this lesion as malignant rather than benign?
qs.e: Invasion of the submucosa is a definitive feature of malignancy. While increased mitotic activity and nuclear pleomorphism are common in malignant cells, they can also be seen in some benign conditions. Formation of glandular structures is characteristic of adenocarcinoma, which can be benign or malignant, but invasion is the key differentiator for malignancy.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - August 28, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: What explains fibre's protective effect against colon cancer?
o: A. Fibre is directly absorbed by colonic epithelial cells, providing anti-cancer nutrients.
D. Fibre promotes the growth of pathogenic bacteria that outcompete harmful strains.
C. Fibre enhances the absorption of dietary carcinogens, leading to their rapid excretion.
B. Fibre reduces colonic transit time, decreasing exposure of the mucosa to potential carcinogens.
qs.e: Fibre, especially insoluble fibre, increases stool bulk and reduces colonic transit time. This decreased transit time means that potential carcinogens present in the faeces have less time to interact with and damage the colonic mucosa, thereby reducing cancer risk. qs.q: A 65-year-old man has a firm mass in the sigmoid colon. Colonoscopy shows an ulcerated lesion with irregular borders. Biopsy demonstrates invasion through the muscularis propria. Which histological feature most strongly distinguishes this lesion as malignant rather than benign?
qs.e: The defining characteristic of malignancy (carcinoma) is invasion through the basement membrane into surrounding stroma or deeper tissues. While benign tumors may show cellular atypia, high mitotic rates, or desmoplasia, only invasion confirms malignancy.

qs.q: Why do cancer cells typically show microsatellite instability (MSI) in hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC)?
qs.e: HNPCC patients have mutations in mismatch repair genes, leading to failure to correct replication errors, particularly in repetitive sequences (microsatellites), causing MSI.

qs.q: In the multistep carcinogenesis model of colon cancer, which genetic alteration typically occurs FIRST?
qs.e: The adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colon cancer typically begins with APC inactivation, followed by KRAS activation, then loss of 18q tumor suppressors, and finally TP53 loss.
qs.s: ONCOPATHOLOGY MCQ EXAMINATION HAllmarks of Cancer 1,2 &3

qs.q: In the adenoma-carcinoma sequence of colon cancer, what is the significance of loss of the tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 18q?
o: It occurs first in the sequence
It occurs in the middle stages between KRAS and TP53 mutations
It is not relevant to colon cancer
qs.e: The multistep progression typically follows: APC loss → KRAS activation → 18q loss → TP53 loss. The 18q loss occurs in intermediate stages of progression.

qs.q: A 70-year-old female with a history of constipation presents with LLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis. CT scan shows a thickened segment of the colon with pericolic fat stranding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Left lower quadrant pain, fever, leukocytosis, and CT findings of a thickened colon segment with pericolic fat stranding are classic for acute diverticulitis, a common condition in the elderly, especially those with a history of constipation.

ai.summary: The colon is the major part of the large intestine, extending from the cecum to the rectum. It is responsible for water and electrolyte absorption and the formation and propulsion of feces.

sections.p: The colon is the major part of the large intestine, extending from the cecum to the rectum. It is responsible for water and electrolyte absorption and the formation and propulsion of feces.

b: Ascending Colon: Retroperitoneal; extends superiorly from the cecum to the right colic (hepatic) flexure.
Transverse Colon: Intraperitoneal; suspended by the transverse mesocolon between the hepatic and splenic flexures.
Descending Colon: Retroperitoneal; extends inferiorly from the left colic (splenic) flexure to the pelvic brim.
Sigmoid Colon: Intraperitoneal; S-shaped segment suspended by the sigmoid mesocolon, terminating at the third sacral vertebra (S3).

sections.p: The colon is distinguished from the small intestine by:
b: Teniae coli: Three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle.
Haustra: Sacculations produced by the shortening of teniae coli.
Omental (epiploic) appendices: Small, fat-filled pouches of peritoneum.
Midgut (up to distal 1/3 of transverse colon): Supplied by the Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA); venous drainage to the SMV; parasympathetic supply via the Vagus nerve (CN X).
Hindgut (distal 1/3 of transverse colon to rectum): Supplied by the Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA); venous drainage to the IMV; parasympathetic supply via Pelvic Splanchnic nerves (S2-S4).
Volvulus: Twisting of the mobile segments (sigmoid or transverse) around their mesentery, leading to bowel obstruction.
Diverticulosis: Herniation of mucosa through muscular defects, most common in the sigmoid colon.
Colorectal Carcinoma: Primarily occurs in the sigmoid colon and rectum; lymphatic spread follows the arterial supply.
Small bowel: Identified by circular folds (plicae circulares) crossing the full width, whereas haustral clefts in the colon are incomplete.
Duodenum: The ascending colon is retroperitoneal like the distal duodenum, but lacks the characteristic C-shape and digestive enzyme inlets.
Abdominal X-rays: Dilated small bowel can mimic the colon if valvulae conniventes are sparse, requiring peripheral vs. central positioning for differentiation.
Referred pain: Early obstruction or inflammation in the midgut-derived colon presents as periumbilical pain rather than localized lower quadrant pain.

faq.q: What are the three cardinal features that distinguish the colon from the small intestine?
faq.a: The colon is identified by the presence of teniae coli (longitudinal muscle bands), haustra (sacculations), and appendices epiploicae (fat-filled peritoneal pouches).

faq.q: Which parts of the colon are located intraperitoneally?
faq.a: The cecum, transverse colon, and sigmoid colon are intraperitoneal and mobile, whereas the ascending and descending colon are primarily retroperitoneal.

faq.q: Where does the transition from midgut to hindgut blood supply occur?
faq.a: The transition occurs at the distal third of the transverse colon, where the superior mesenteric artery supply ends and the inferior mesenteric artery begins.
